action_criteria.label: Structured informant history and bedside cognitive screen scored against the Rascovsky features

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe social-cognition impairment with preserved memory, naming and visuospatial function
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including executive and social-cognition measures
action_criteria.rationale: A near-normal screen understates the syndrome; social-cognition and real-world executive testing show the deficit.

action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproate trough therapeutic (68 mcg/mL); ammonia only mildly raised (38 umol/L) with normal liver chemistry
action_criteria.label: Valproate level and serum ammonia
action_criteria.rationale: Valproate can cause hyperammonaemic encephalopathy even at therapeutic levels; the level and ammonia exclude it before the syndrome is attributed to neurodegeneration.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No definite frontal or anterior temporal atrophy and no structural lesion

action_criteria.rationale: Excludes a structural or vascular cause; a normal or near-normal MRI does not exclude bvFTD.

action_criteria.rationale: With a normal or equivocal MRI, functional imaging is the imaging support that probable bvFTD requires.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
Do not stop or switch valproate on account of the mildly raised ammonia alone: it does not explain the syndrome and his bipolar disorder has been stable on it for 15 years.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state the features present (disinhibition, apathy, stereotyped behaviour, dysexecutive profile), the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible on the clinical features with a normal MRI; probable once functional imaging shows frontal hypometabolism; definite if a pathogenic variant is found), and state that a normal MRI does not exclude bvFTD.

Explain why bipolar relapse does not account for the syndrome: the phenotype differs from his previous hypomanic episodes (no pressured speech, reduced need for sleep or increased creativity), the course is progressive and unremitting, and insight is lost; coordinate the plan with his psychiatrist.

State that valproate toxicity is excluded: the trough is therapeutic and the mildly raised ammonia with normal liver chemistry does not explain an 18-month progressive syndrome, so valproate, which has kept him stable for 15 years, need not be stopped.
Address safety and capacity in a man who lives alone: finances and contracts, driving, sexual disinhibition and public social media posting; arrange support and a named contact.
Offer genetic counselling given his father's institutional decline in his 50s under a psychiatric label, before any genetic test and before any predictive testing of relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not part of the FTD work-up; FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT is the functional study when one is needed.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

behavioural variant frontotemporal demen.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. New behavioural change in mid-life with progressive functional decline should prompt a neurodegenerative work-up even in a person with a psychiatric history. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle bvFTD with a normal MRI, misattributed to bipolar disorder, on valproate. Teaching: a normal MRI does not exclude bvFTD and functional imaging gives the imaging support; social-cognition testing shows the deficit a near-normal screen misses; valproate toxicity is excluded by level and ammonia; a parent's late-onset psychiatric diagnosis may be misdiagnosed FTD. The optional gene panel shows a C9orf72 expansion, which is associated with slowly progressive bvFTD and little atrophy.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F is a 54-year-old published novelist with a 15-year history of bipolar disorder type II (well-controlled on valproate) and hypothyroidism who is referred by his psychiatrist for neurological evaluation. His psychiatrist refers him with a note: 'progressive behavioral changes that feel different from prior bipolar episodes; patient does not recognize or endorse symptoms; consider organic process.' Over the past 18 months, Mr. F has undergone a behavioral transformation that his former partner (they divorced 2 years ago) and publisher have independently noticed. His publisher, with whom he has had a relationship for 12 years, reports that his correspondence has become strange: he sends the same paragraph from his current manuscript in every email, verbatim, regardless of the question asked. His manuscript, which he has been working on for 3 years, consists of the same 2,000 words rearranged repeatedly. He is unaware that this is unusual and insists the work is 'progressing.' He has posted a series of publicly embarrassing social media messages commenting on strangers' physical appearances and has made several sexually inappropriate advances toward his publisher's assistant, dismissing any attempt to discuss this as 'censorship.' He has developed an extraordinary fixation on a single television crime drama, watching it for 8 to 14 hours per day and quoting it verbatim in conversations. He is meticulous about eating the same three foods in the same sequence every day. He has lost all interest in the literary community, which was central to his identity and social world. He does not recognize any of these behaviors as problematic. His bipolar disorder has never manifested this way: his prior hypomanic episodes were characterized by rapid speech, reduced need for sleep, and increased creativity, not perseverative repetition and social disinhibition. He has no history of psychosis. His father was institutionalized in his 50s with a diagnosis of 'late-onset schizophrenia.' He manages his own affairs and lives alone; his former partner and publisher are the main informants.
